extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent examiners, policymakers, and academics
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for determining when a piece of information constitutes prior art for novelty and inventive-step (non-obviousness) assessments in patent law, covering means, timing, place, persons, recipients, new media, evidentiary burdens, and related procedural aspects across jurisdictions (notably United States, Uruguay, Venezuela/Andean Community).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognized means of disclosure (U.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 102 of the United States patent laws sets forth the recognized means of disclosure that may constitute prior art: patents, printed publications, pending United States patent applications, offers for sale in the United States, and prior knowledge or use in the United States. See 35 U.S.C. § 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories are the canonical forms of prior art under U.S. law; the analysis of a putative disclosure should map it to one of these forms when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration required for oral testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral testimony offered to establish prior knowledge, use or invention, particularly when provided by interested persons, generally requires corroborating testimony or evidence and will not alone support a finding of lack of novelty or of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat oral statements skeptically unless supported by independent documentary or witness corroboration (standard applied in prosecution and litigation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Age of patent/publication does not defeat prior art effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent or publication serves as a prior art disclosure, which may be used to assess novelty and obviousness, no matter how old the patent or publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even long-unheeded patents/publications can invalidate newer patents (citing Western States Mach. Co. v. S. S. Hepworth Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost art / evidentiary unavailability
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior knowledge or prior use may fall into the category of 'lost art' and become unavailable as prior art because evidence of such prior knowledge or prior use is no longer available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where documentary or testimonial evidence cannot be produced, an asserted prior use/knowledge may fail for lack of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place requirement for prior knowledge/use (U.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior knowledge, use, sale or invention not embodied in a patent or printed publication serves as prior art only if it occurs in the United States. A prior patent or printed publication serves as prior art regardless of the country in which it is disclosed. (35 U.S.C. §§ 102(a) & (b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between 'printed publication/patent' (worldwide) and 'knowledge/use' (must be in U.S.) when analyzing geographic scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentionality/accident of disclosure irrelevant (U.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: No distinction is made in considering whether something constitutes a prior art disclosure under United States patent law as to whether the disclosure was made intentionally or accidentally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on whether the disclosure met publicness/other legal criteria, not on the actor's intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor's own disclosures and §102(a) exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant’s own prior original work cannot anticipate his own later invention under section 102(a). One’s own work is not prior art under section 102(a) even though it has been disclosed to the public in a manner or form which otherwise would fall under § 102(a) (e.g. In re Katz).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate disclosures made by the inventor from disclosures by others; consider statutory grace provisions and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-year grace period for inventor disclosures (§102(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 102(b) provides for a one year grace period for an inventor’s disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosures attributable to the inventor within one year before filing/priority date may be excluded from prior art under U.S. law; check exact statutory/claiming dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pending U.S. patent applications as prior art (§102(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 102(e) pending United States patent applications require disclosure 'by another' and may constitute prior art once published (or as statutorily provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat earlier-filed U.S. applications (and their disclosures) as potential prior art against later applications under the statutory framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breach of confidentiality does not negate prior art effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a putative inventor may have legal remedies against a party who discloses information in breach of a confidentiality agreement, a disclosure that otherwise satisfies the requirements of section 102 would constitute prior art even if made in breach of a confidentiality agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidentiality agreements may give contractual remedies but do not necessarily prevent a disclosure from qualifying as prior art if it becomes publicly accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement for prior art disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: For a disclosure to constitute prior art for novelty and obviousness analyses, the disclosure must enable one of ordinary skill in the art to comprehend and make the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the prior disclosure provides sufficient detail (enablement) to practice the claimed invention; prior art need not teach well-known skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality agreements affect publicness
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of a confidentiality agreement or a finding of implied confidentiality is considered in determining whether a use is 'public' under §§102(a) and (b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidential presentations or documents under confidentiality are less likely to qualify as public prior art; examine contractual terms and implied confidentiality facts (citing Fujitsu).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad construction of 'printed publication' for internet disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'printed publication' has been broadly construed in the United States (e.g., In re Wyer); a document is a printed publication if it is 'available and accessible to the persons concerned with the art' whether on microfilm, magnetic media, or the web.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An internet disclosure that is publicly accessible (e.g., indexed by search engines, archived) can be treated as a printed publication for prior art purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing/searchability as factor for internet public accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Some method would be required to provide public accessibility to information on the internet, such as indexing of the information by a search engine to permit access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the specific internet posting was discoverable by those skilled in the art (indexing, linking, known URL distribution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Private email disclosures do not constitute public prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of information in private e-mails should not constitute sufficient disclosure to affect novelty or inventive step (non-obviousness), as such information is not publicly accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish private electronic communications from public web postings; consider recipients and access controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encryption/passwords and payment controls considered for public accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The encryption of information should be considered in determining whether the information is publicly accessible. Whether payment is required to view the information does not appear to be important in determining its public availability provided that the information is available to anyone concerned with the art who is willing to pay the fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If encryption or access-control maintains confidentiality, the item likely is not prior art; paywalls do not necessarily prevent prior art status if access is broadly available to skilled persons willing to pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place-of-access analysis for internet disclosures (U.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: For prior knowledge or use to constitute prior art under United States patent law, the information must be known or used in the United States. For internet disclosures, the proper analysis likely is whether the information was publicly accessible to those concerned with the art in the United States, not whether the content originated from a U.S. server.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess practical accessibility to U.S.-based skilled practitioners rather than server location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing/duration requirement for electronic disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: The information should appear on the internet long enough so that it is accessible to the public; this should be decided on a case-by-case basis considering factors such as how often the particular web site is accessed. Archives are desirable to establish what material was placed on the internet and when.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short-lived postings may be harder to prove/publicly accessible; archiving (e.g., Wayback, cached copies) strengthens evidentiary showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for internet disclosures (prosecution vs infringement)
rubrics_metrics.description: During prosecution, the United States Patent Office should have the burden of proving that the information was disclosed. In an infringement action, the accused infringer who is seeking to invalidate the patent should have the burden of proving that the information was disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate evidentiary burdens according to the proceeding type; request documentary evidence or internet archives accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: No need for different substantive rules for internet disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: No need exists for different rules to determine whether a specific piece of information was disclosed on the internet; the same rules applicable for oral disclosure, including a requirement for corroboration of oral testimony, may be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply existing evidentiary and publicness tests to new media, while adapting proof methods (archives, logs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign patents may constitute prior art under §102(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign patents (e.g., German Geschmacksmuster, Danish 'eneret') have been held to qualify as patents within the meaning of the statute and can constitute prior art (In re Carlson; Atlas Glass Co. v. Simonds). If a foreign patent does not confer rights sufficient to qualify as a patent under §102(a), it may nevertheless constitute prior art as a prior printed publication so long as it meets the requirements of that form of disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a foreign registered design/patent confers patent-like exclusive rights or otherwise meets printed-publication criteria for prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uruguay: 'state of the art' = publicly made known and executable
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 9 of Uruguay's Patent Act: 'state of the art' means know-how made known to the public before filing/priority by oral or written description or any other means, within the country or abroad, 'so that said know-how can be executed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uruguay explicitly requires that disclosed know-how be capable of execution; examine sufficiency to enable practice in that jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uruguay: publication triggers 60-day observation period and searches
rubrics_metrics.description: An official search as to anticipations is conducted among PCT, US and national archives; publication of an application in the Industrial Property Bulletin opens a term of 60 days within which any interested party may file observations, including citations of disclosed and relevant prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural requirement: monitor official bulletins and participate in observatory periods to submit prior art citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uruguay: one-year grace period for inventor-originated disclosures (Article 10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 10: 'Novelty shall not be affected by the disclosure of the invention made within the term of one year before the filing date ... providing said disclosure comes directly or indirectly from actions performed by the inventor as well as by his/her heirs or by third parties, based on information obtained directly or indirectly from said inventor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uruguay provides a grace similar to other systems if disclosure is traceable to the inventor; confirm applicability based on origin of disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uruguay: confidentiality breach sanctions for Office staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles 120 and 121 impose confidentiality obligations on Industrial Property Office employees and penalties (dismissal, contract cancellation, fines) for violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative safeguards exist to protect unpublished application information; consider enforcement remedies in cases of improper disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venezuela/Andean Community: Article 17 grace/exclusion conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision 486 Article 17: no account shall be taken of any disclosure during the year prior to filing (or priority) if the disclosure was attributable to (i) the inventor or assignee, (ii) a competent national office that published the application in contravention, or (iii) a third party who obtained the information directly or indirectly from the inventor or assignee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regional rule carving out certain inventor-attributable disclosures from being treated as damaging prior art during a one-year period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venezuela/Andean Community: inventive step test (Article 18)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention involves an inventive step if, for a person in the trade with average skills in the technical field concerned, the said invention is neither obvious nor obviously derived from the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the 'person having ordinary skill in the art' (PHOSITA) obviousness standard in inventive-step assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venezuela: pending unpublished applications generally do not affect novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: If the application is not yet published it will have no effect on the assessment of novelty. However Article 16 makes the contents of an earlier-filed pending application part of the state of the art for novelty under certain publication/timing conditions (e.g., 18 months rule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat pending applications as potential prior art only pursuant to statutory provisions about earlier filings/publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venezuela: broad list of recognized means of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Products or processes already patented and everything that has been made available to the public by written or oral description, use, marketing, or any other means prior to the filing date are part of the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law enumerates multiple channels that can create prior art; consider commercial use and marketing as well as publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venezuela: evidentiary burdens for internet disclosures and suggestion for different standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The person who states that a specific piece of information was disclosed on the internet should have the burden of proof. There should be equivalent levels of evidence for different ways of disclosure. The potential manipulation of information disclosed through new media suggests there should be different standards for the recognition of such disclosure, although locally no such rules exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting internet prior art in that jurisdiction, prepare to show proof (archives, logs); consider arguments on appropriate evidentiary standards for electronic media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venezuela: place-of-disclosure and applicable law
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicable law for determining whether a disclosure has occurred is the law of the country in which novelty and inventive step is assessed; the law does not make any difference on place of disclosure in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply local substantive law to determine publicness and effect of foreign/online disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse engineering and ability-to-understand thresholds (varies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions whether the possibility that a person might obtain the information through additional steps, such as disassembly of embodiments or reverse engineering, is sufficient to constitute a disclosure produce varied answers: U.S. rule emphasizes enablement to one of ordinary skill; some jurisdictions (Venezuela) said 'No' to reverse engineering being sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the disclosed product or embodiment enables reproduction by PHOSITA, and check local case law/statute on reverse engineering as a route to public disclosure.
